title: Authorization
summary: Knowing who someone is doesn’t tell you what they may see or do. Checking that, everywhere.

steps.title: Logged in is not the same as allowed
body: Eve, from another company, is a legitimate user. She opens her invoice at /invoices/1042, changes the number to 1043 — and sees an invoice belonging to Acme.
The API checked that she was logged in, never that this invoice was hers. This is broken object-level authorization — the most common API security flaw.

callout.text: Hiding a button in the UI is not authorization. Attackers call your API directly, with any id they like.

steps.title: Check ownership on every request
body: Every lookup must be scoped to who is asking: fetch invoice 1043 only if it belongs to the caller’s organisation. For Eve that finds nothing, and she gets 404 Not Found.
Deny by default: any endpoint that forgets the check should fail closed, not open.

callout.text: Answer 404, not 403, for other people’s objects — don’t confirm they exist. Random ids (UUIDs) help, but are no substitute for the check.

changes: + Queries scoped to the caller’s organisation

steps.title: Case: “role”: “admin”
body: Eve edits her own profile — that’s allowed. But the API takes the JSON body and saves every field in it. So she adds "role": "admin" to the request and promotes herself.
This is mass assignment. Fix: each endpoint has an allow-list of fields it may change, and roles change only through a separate admin-only endpoint.

callout.text: Frameworks that bind request bodies straight onto database models make this easy to get wrong. Be explicit about writable fields.

changes: − API saves it · Eve is admin

steps.title: Let the database enforce tenants too
body: Ownership checks live in application code, so one query that forgets AND org_id = … brings the leak right back. Add a second layer: row-level security in the database.
The app tells each connection which organisation it is serving; the database then filters every query by that org. Even SELECT * FROM invoices only returns the caller’s rows.

callout.text: Defence in depth: assume any single check will eventually be forgotten, and make sure a second one is there.

changes: ~ App sets the caller’s org per connection

steps.title: Roles: what each kind of user may do
body: Inside Acme, people need different powers: some only view invoices, some edit them, a few approve large ones. Rather than list permissions per person, group them into roles and give each person a role — role-based access control (RBAC).
Alice is an accountant: she can edit invoices but not approve them.

callout.text: Keep roles few and meaningful. Hundreds of special-case roles become impossible to reason about.

steps.title: Relationships: sharing and teams
body: Roles struggle with sharing: “Alice can see this folder because it was shared with her team”. Relationship-based access (ReBAC) stores facts like “invoice 1042 is in folder Q3”, “Q3 is shared with team Finance”, “Alice is in Finance”, and follows the chain.
This is how Google Docs-style sharing works at scale.

callout.text: Google’s Zanzibar paper popularised this model; SpiceDB and OpenFGA are open-source versions.

steps.title: Decide in one place
body: Permission checks scattered as if-statements across twenty services drift apart, and nobody can answer “who can approve invoices?”. Instead, each service asks a policy service: “may Alice edit invoice 1042?”, and enforces the yes or no.
The rules live in one place, are tested like code, and every decision can be logged.

callout.text: Tools: Open Policy Agent (Rego), AWS Cedar, or a permissions service like SpiceDB. Cache decisions briefly to keep calls fast.

steps.title: Case: a service with keys to everything
body: The reports service connects to the database with the admin account — it was quickest to set up. One day a SQL-injection bug is found in a report filter.
Because the service could read every table, the attacker dumps users, password hashes and payment details too — not just invoices.

callout.text: A component’s permissions define the blast radius of its bugs.

changes: + Reports service with admin DB credentials

steps.title: Least privilege
body: Give every service — and every person — only the access its job needs. The reports service gets a read-only account that can see the invoices view and nothing else; each service has its own credentials and identity.
The same injection bug now leaks, at worst, invoices the service could already read — and alarms fire when it tries anything else.

callout.text: Apply it everywhere: database grants, cloud IAM roles, API scopes, and staff access (time-limited, approved, logged).

steps.title: Case: the confused deputy
body: Alice asks for a report of invoices over $10,000. The API hands the job to the reports service, which queries with its own identity — and it may read every tenant’s invoices. Alice’s report includes Globex’s.
The reports service was tricked into using its authority on someone else’s behalf: a confused deputy.

callout.text: Whenever a service acts for a user, ask: whose permissions apply here — the service’s or the user’s?

changes: + Report runs as the reports service

steps.title: Act as the user, not as yourself
body: Pass the user’s identity along: the API forwards Alice’s token (or exchanges it for a narrower one), and the reports service runs the query as Alice — with her organisation and her permissions.
The service’s own powerful credentials are only used for things no user asked for, like nightly maintenance.

callout.text: OAuth token exchange and service meshes can carry the end user’s identity across every hop automatically.

steps.title: Audit logs: who saw what
body: Finally, record every access to sensitive data — who, what, when, from where — in an append-only audit log that the people being audited can’t edit.
It answers “who looked at this customer’s invoices?” after an incident, and powers alerts: a support agent opening 5,000 invoices in ten minutes is worth a page.

callout.text: Audit logs are also required by most compliance standards (SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR requests).

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Check that the caller may access this object, on every request.
  • Use roles for kinds of users, relationships for sharing.
  • Decide in a central policy; enforce in each service.
  • Allow-list writable fields; add row-level security as a second layer.
  • Grant least privilege; act as the user, not as the service; keep an audit log.

callout.text: Next up: Encryption & Secrets — protecting data on the wire, on disk, and the keys themselves.
